Pas-dammim means “edge of blood.” It seems that part of the story of Shammah, another hero, is joined here (2 Samuel 23:11-12). In Samuel the field had lentils.
Adullam may mean “hiding place.” Rephaim means “ghosts” or “giants.”
The Syriac version says “the Thirty” here and in verse 21.
Or “Among the Three he was given double honor.”
The Hebrew says “two Ariel of Moab.” Ariel means “lion of God.” It may mean “two champions.”
Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.” Kabzeel means “God gathers.”
The Hebrew says “five cubits.” A cubit was about 18 inches.
Elhanan means “God is kind.” Asahel means “God has made.”
2 Samuel 23:25 has “Shammah from Harod.” Shammoth means “ruins.”
Ira means “watchful.” Ikkesh means “crooked.”
2 Samuel 23:27-28 has Mebunnai and Zalmon.
Maharai means “quick.” Heled means “lifetime.”
2 Samuel 23:29 has Ittai. Ribai means “Yahweh argues the case.” Gibeah means “hill.”
2 Samuel 23:30-31 has Hiddai and Abi-albon. Gaash means “shaking.” Abiel means “God is father.”
Eliahba means “God hides.” Shaalbon means “place of foxes.”
2 Samuel 23:32-33 has “the sons of Jashen” and Shammah. Hashem means “name.”
Ahiam means “mother’s brother.” Sachar means “reward.” Ur means “flame.”
2 Samuel 23:34 has different names here.
Hezro means “walled place.” Naarai means “young.”
2 Samuel 23:36 has Igal and Bani the Gadite. Mibhar means “choice.”
Zelek means “crack.” Ammon means “people.” Beeroth means “wells.”
Gareb means “scabby.”
2 Samuel 23:39 ends the list with Uriah. Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
Adina means “delicate.” The words “with his thirty men” may mean “and thirty were over him.”
Joshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
Uzzia means “Yahweh is my strength.” Shama means “he heard.” Aroer means “juniper.”
Jediael means “known by God.”
Jeribai means “Yahweh argues the case.” Elnaam means “God is pleasant.” Ithmah means “loss.”
Jaasiel means “God makes.” Zobah may mean “station.”

subheads.1: David Becomes King of All Israel

verses.text: Here are the men who joined David at Ziklag back when he had to stay hidden from Saul, Kish’s son.{a} They were among the brave fighters who helped David in battle.
They carried bows. They could shoot arrows and sling stones with either hand, left or right. They belonged to Benjamin’s tribe, the same tribe as Saul.{b}
Their leader was Ahiezer, and next was Joash. Both were sons of Shemaah from Gibeah. Others were Jeziel and Pelet, Azmaveth’s sons; Beracah; and Jehu from Anathoth.{c}
Ishmaiah from Gibeon was a hero among the Thirty and also one of their leaders. With them were Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, and Jozabad from Gederah.{d}
Then came Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah and Shemariah, and Shephatiah from Haruph,{e}
also five men of Korah’s clan: Elkanah and Isshiah, Azarel and Joezer, and Jashobeam,{f}
and Joelah and Zebadiah, whose father was Jeroham from Gedor.{g}

Some men from Gad’s tribe left Saul and went over to David at his fort in the desert. They were tough, trained soldiers, skilled with shield and spear. Their faces were fierce like a lion’s, and on the hills they could run as fast as deer.{h}
Ezer was their leader. Obadiah was second in rank, and Eliab third.{i}
Fourth was Mishmannah, and fifth was Jeremiah.{j}
Sixth came Attai, and seventh Eliel.{k}
Eighth came Johanan, and ninth Elzabad.{l}
Tenth was another Jeremiah, and eleventh was Machbannai.{m}
These Gadites were army officers. The weakest could take on a hundred men, and the strongest could take on a thousand.{n}
In early spring, when the Jordan River was flooding over its banks, these men crossed it.{o} They made everyone living in the valleys run away, to the east and to the west.
More men, from the tribes of Benjamin and Judah, made their way to David’s fort.

David went out to greet them. He said, “If you’ve come as friends to help me, then my heart is with you, and we will stand together. But if you’ve come to betray me to my enemies, even though I’ve done nothing wrong, may the God our fathers worshiped see it and punish you.”

Then God’s Spirit came over Amasai, who later led the Thirty.{p} He called out, “David, we belong to you! Son of Jesse, we stand with you! May all go well for you and for everyone who helps you. Your God is the one helping you.” David took them in and gave them command of his raiding troops.

Some men from Manasseh’s tribe also came over to David. This happened when David went along with the Philistines to fight Saul. But in the end David did not help them. The Philistine rulers talked it over and sent him away. They said, “He’ll go back to his old master Saul, and it will cost us our lives.”{q}
As David headed back to Ziklag, these men from Manasseh joined him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, another Jozabad, Elihu and Zillethai. Each had commanded a thousand soldiers in Manasseh.{r}
They helped David fight against bands of raiders.{s} They were all brave fighters, and they became leaders in his army.
Day after day, new helpers kept coming to join David. In time his army became huge, as great as God’s own army.{t}
These are the numbers of soldiers, armed for battle, who came to David at Hebron. They came to give Saul’s kingdom to David, just as Yahweh had promised.{u}
Judah sent 6,800 armed men who carried shields and spears.
Simeon sent 7,100 brave soldiers ready for war.
Levi sent 4,600 men.
Jehoiada, head of Aaron’s family, came with 3,700 men.{v}
Also came Zadok, a strong young fighter, bringing 22 commanders from his father’s family.{w}
Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe, sent 3,000 men. Until then most of them had stayed loyal to Saul’s family.
Ephraim sent 20,800 brave soldiers. Each was well known in his own family.
Half of Manasseh’s tribe sent 18,000 men. Each was chosen by name to come and crown David king.
Issachar sent 200 leaders, with all the relatives they commanded. These leaders understood the times and knew the right thing for Israel to do.{x}
Zebulun sent 50,000 trained soldiers. They knew how to use every kind of weapon and how to line up for battle. They came to help David{y} with complete loyalty.
Naphtali sent 1,000 officers, along with 37,000 men who carried shields and spears.
Dan sent 28,600 men ready for battle.
Asher sent 40,000 trained soldiers ready for battle.
Across the Jordan to the east, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the other half of Manasseh sent 120,000 men with all kinds of weapons.{z}

All these fighting men, ready to take their places in the battle line, came to Hebron. They were fully determined to make David king of all Israel. Everyone else in Israel agreed that David should be king.
For three days the men feasted there with David. Their relatives had sent food for them.

People from nearby, and from as far away as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali, packed food onto their animals, whether donkey, camel, mule or ox, and brought it. There was flour, cakes of figs and of raisins, wine, olive oil, and herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, more than enough. Everyone in Israel was full of joy.

notes.text: Ziklag may mean “winding.” See 1 Samuel 27:6. This chapter is not found in Samuel.
Benjamin means “son of the right hand,” so it is worth noting that these men were skilled with the left hand too (compare Judges 20:16).
Some Hebrew copies spell Jeziel as Jezuel. Ahiezer means “my brother is help.” Beracah means “blessing.” Jehu means “Yahweh is he.”
In Hebrew, verse 4 is split into verses 4 and 5, so from here on the Hebrew verse numbers are one higher. Ishmaiah means “Yahweh hears.” Jahaziel means “God sees.” Gederah means “sheep pen.”
Some Hebrew copies say Hariphite. Eluzai means “God is my strength.” Bealiah means “Yahweh is lord.” Shemariah means “Yahweh guards.”
Azarel means “God helps.” Joezer means “Yahweh is help.” These Korahites may have been a family in Benjamin with that name, not the Levites.
Joelah may mean “may he help.” Gedor means “wall.”
Gad means “good fortune.” The Hebrew word for “deer” means “gazelles.”
Ezer means “help.”
Mishmannah means “richness.”
The meaning of Attai is uncertain.
Elzabad means “God has given.”
Machbannai may mean “dressed in a cloak.”
Or “The least was over a hundred, and the greatest over a thousand.”
The Hebrew says “the first month.” This is the month of Nisan, in March and April, at barley harvest time, when the Jordan floods (Joshua 3:15).
Some Hebrew copies say “the officers.” Amasai means “load carrier.” He may be the Amasa of 2 Samuel 17:25.
See 1 Samuel 29:1-11. Manasseh means “making forget.”
Adnah means “joy.” Elihu means “he is my God.”
These were probably the Amalekite raiders of 1 Samuel 30.
Or “a very great army.”
Verses 23-37 are found only in Chronicles. Some think the Hebrew word for “thousand” here means a “unit” of soldiers.
Jehoiada was probably the father of Benaiah (11:22).
Zadok later became high priest.
Issachar may mean “there is a reward.”
The word “David” comes from the Septuagint. Zebulun means “home.”
Reuben means “look, a son.”

subheads.1: Men Who Joined David at Ziklag
subheads.23: The Army That Made David King

verses.text: David talked things over with all his officers, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and with every leader.

Then he spoke to all the Israelites gathered there. “If this plan seems good to you,” he said, “and if Yahweh our God wants it, let’s send word everywhere. Let’s call all our relatives who stayed home across Israel’s land. Let’s call the priests and Levites too, in the towns where they live with their grasslands. Let’s ask them all to come and join us.
Then let’s bring God’s ark back here with us. While Saul was king, we paid no attention to it.”{a}
Everyone there agreed to do it, since they all thought it was the right plan.
So David called together all the Israelites, from the Shihor River on Egypt’s border all the way north to Lebo-hamath. Their goal was to carry God’s ark away from Kiriath-jearim.{b}

David led all of them up to Baalah, which is Kiriath-jearim in Judah. They went to bring back the ark of God. It is called by the name of Yahweh, who sits on his throne between the winged creatures.{c}
They set God’s ark on a brand-new cart and moved it away from Abinadab’s house. Uzza and Ahio guided the cart.{d}
David and all the people celebrated in front of God as hard as they could. They sang songs and played music on harps of every kind, tambourines, cymbals and trumpets.
They came to Chidon’s threshing floor, and there the oxen stumbled. Uzza put out his hand and took hold of the ark to keep it from falling.{e}
Yahweh became very angry with Uzza for touching the ark, and he struck him down. Uzza died right there in God’s presence.
David was upset that Yahweh’s anger had burst out against Uzza. To this day that spot is called Perez-uzza.{f}
That day David became afraid of God. He asked, “How can I ever bring God’s ark to my home?”
David decided not to bring the ark home to his own city. Instead he had it taken to the house of Obed-edom, a man from Gath.{g}
For the next three months God’s ark stayed at Obed-edom’s home with his family. Yahweh poured out good things on that household and on everything Obed-edom had.

notes.text: Verses 5-14 are much like 2 Samuel 6:1-11. Verses 1-4 appear only in Chronicles.
The Shihor was probably a branch of the Nile River or the stream on Egypt’s border. Lebo-hamath means “the entrance to Hamath.” Kiriath-jearim means “town of forests.”
Baalah means “lady.” 2 Samuel 6:2 calls it Baale-judah. The winged creatures are cherubim, heavenly guards shaped as figures on the ark’s lid.
Uzza means “strength.” Ahio may mean “his brother.”
2 Samuel 6:6 calls it Nacon. Chidon may mean “spear.”
Perez-uzza means “burst out against Uzza.”
Obed-edom means “servant of Edom.” Gath means “winepress.”

subheads.1: David Tries to Move the Ark

verses.text: Hiram, who ruled Tyre, sent men to David with cedar logs, along with builders skilled in stone and wood, to put up a palace for him.{a}
Then David understood that Yahweh had made his rule over Israel secure. Yahweh had made his kingdom great for the good of his people Israel.
David took still more wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
The children born to him there were named Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,{b}
Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,{c}
Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.{d}
News reached the Philistines that David had been anointed as king over all Israel. So their whole army marched out to hunt for him. As soon as David learned of it, he marched out to face them.
The Philistines had come and attacked the Rephaim Valley.
David prayed, “Shall I go up and fight the Philistines? Will you give me victory over them?” Yahweh told him, “Yes, attack! I will hand them over to you.”

So David’s army went up to Baal-perazim and beat the Philistines there. David said, “Like water bursting through a dam, God has burst through my enemies by my hand.” So that place was named Baal-perazim.{e}
The Philistines left their idols behind on the battlefield. David gave orders to burn them up.{f}
Some time later the Philistines came back and attacked the valley once more.
Again David asked God what to do. God answered, “Don’t go straight up at them. Go around and come at them from behind, near the balsam trees.{g}
Listen for a sound like marching feet in the treetops. When you hear it, go out and fight. It will be a sign that God is marching ahead of you to crush the Philistine forces.”
David followed God’s orders. His men struck down Philistine soldiers from Gibeon clear to Gezer.{h}
David became famous in every land. Yahweh made every nation afraid of him.

notes.text: Verses 1-16 are much like 2 Samuel 5:11-25. Hiram may mean “my brother is lifted up.” Tyre means “rock.”
Compare 3:5-8. Shammua means “heard.”
Elpelet is the same as Eliphelet in 3:6. Elishua means “God saves.”
Beeliada means “the Lord knows.” In 3:8 he is called Eliada, “God knows.”
Baal-perazim means “the Lord breaks through.”
2 Samuel 5:21 says David’s men carried the idols away. Deuteronomy 7:5, 25 commands that idols be burned.
The exact kind of tree is not known.
2 Samuel 5:25 says “from Geba.” Gezer means “share.”

verses.text: David built houses for himself in his city. He also got a place ready for God’s ark and set up a tent to hold it.
Then David gave this order: “No one but the Levites may carry God’s ark. Yahweh picked them for this task and to serve him for all time.”{a}
So all Israel was summoned to Jerusalem by David to bring Yahweh’s ark up to the place he had made ready for it.
He brought together Aaron’s descendants and the other Levites.
From Kohath’s clan came Uriel, their leader, with 120 relatives.{b}
From Merari’s clan came Asaiah, their leader, with 220 relatives.{c}
From Gershom’s clan came Joel, their leader, with 130 relatives.{d}
From Elizaphan’s clan came Shemaiah, their leader, with 200 relatives.{e}
From Hebron’s clan came Eliel, their leader, with 80 relatives.{f}
From Uzziel’s clan came Amminadab, their leader, with 112 relatives.{g}
Then David sent for the priests Zadok and Abiathar. He also called in six Levite leaders: Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel and Amminadab.{h}
“You lead the Levite families,” he said. “Make yourselves pure and holy, you and the other Levites. Then bring up the ark of Yahweh, Israel’s God, to the spot I have prepared for it.
Last time, it was not you Levites who carried it. That is why Yahweh our God burst out in anger against us. We did not ask him how it should be done.”
So the priests and Levites made themselves clean and ready to carry up the ark of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
The Levites lifted God’s ark with its poles resting on their shoulders. That was the way Moses had ordered, following Yahweh’s word.{i}
David told the Levite leaders to choose men from their families to be singers. These men were to play harps, lyres and cymbals loudly and sing happy songs.
The Levites named Heman, whose father was Joel. Next they named Asaph, Berechiah’s son, one of Heman’s relatives. From their relatives in Merari’s clan they chose Ethan son of Kushaiah.{j}

Next in rank came their relatives Zechariah,{k} Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu and Mikneiah. The gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel were also with them.{l}
Heman, Asaph and Ethan, the singers, were chosen to crash the bronze cymbals.
Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah and Benaiah played harps tuned high, in the alamoth style.{m}
Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel and Azaziah led the music with lyres tuned low, in the sheminith style.{n}
Chenaniah, a Levite leader, was in charge of carrying the ark. He taught the others how to do it, because he knew the job well.{o}
Berechiah and Elkanah guarded the doorway of the ark’s tent.{p}

Seven priests marched in front of God’s ark blowing trumpets: Shebaniah and Joshaphat, Nethanel and Amasai, plus Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer. Two more men, Obed-edom and Jehiah, also guarded the ark’s doorway.{q}
So David, Israel’s leaders and the commanders of thousands went with great joy to Obed-edom’s house. They went to bring up the ark that held Yahweh’s covenant.{r}
God helped the Levites who carried the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, and so they offered up seven bulls and seven rams.{s}
David’s robe was of fine linen. All the Levites carrying the ark wore the same, and so did the singers, and Chenaniah, the leader of their singing.{t} David also had on a linen ephod.
So all the Israelites brought up the ark of Yahweh’s covenant. They shouted for joy and blew rams’ horns and trumpets. They crashed cymbals and played loud music on harps and lyres.
As the ark of Yahweh’s covenant came into David’s City, Saul’s daughter Michal looked down through a window. She watched King David leaping and dancing for joy, and deep inside she hated him.{u}

notes.text: See Numbers 4:15 and Deuteronomy 10:8. Levi means “joined.”
Uriel means “God is my light.”
Asaiah means “Yahweh has made.”
Gershom is also spelled Gershon.
Elizaphan, meaning “God has hidden,” was a Kohathite (Numbers 3:30). Shemaiah means “Yahweh has heard.”
Eliel means “my God is God.”
Amminadab means “my people are willing.”
Abiathar means “the father has plenty.”
See Exodus 25:14 and Numbers 7:9.
Kushaiah is called Kishi in 6:44.
The Hebrew adds “Ben,” which means “son.” It is probably a copying mistake. It is missing in the Septuagint and in verse 20.
Jaaziel, called Aziel in verse 20, means “God makes strong.” Jehiel means “God lives.” Maaseiah means “work of Yahweh.” Mikneiah means “Yahweh owns.”
Alamoth means “young women.” It is probably a music term for high notes (compare the heading of Psalm 46).
Sheminith means “the eighth.” It is probably a music term for low notes or for an eight-string instrument (compare the headings of Psalms 6 and 12). Azaziah means “Yahweh is strong.”
Or “was in charge of the singing … he taught singing.” The Hebrew word can mean “carrying” or “lifting up the voice.” Chenaniah means “Yahweh makes firm.”
Elkanah means “God has created.”
Shebaniah means “Yahweh has brought back.” Nethanel means “God has given.” Jehiah means “Yahweh lives.”
Verses 25-29 are much like 2 Samuel 6:12-16.
2 Samuel 6:13 says that after the carriers had taken six steps, David sacrificed a bull and a fat calf.
An ephod was a linen vest worn by priests. The words “the singers” may have been added by a copier.
Michal means “who is like God?”

subheads.1: Getting Ready to Move the Ark

verses.text: They carried God’s ark inside and set it down in the tent David had put up for it. Then they brought burnt offerings and peace offerings to God.{a}
When David was done with all the offerings, he asked Yahweh to bless the people, speaking in Yahweh’s name.
Then he handed out food to every Israelite there, men and women alike. Each person received bread, a share of meat{b} and a cake made of raisins.
David picked some Levites to serve in front of Yahweh’s ark. Their job was to call on Yahweh, Israel’s God, and to thank him and praise him.

Asaph was their leader. Zechariah was next in rank, and then came Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom and Jeiel. These men played harps and lyres, and Asaph crashed the cymbals.{c}
The priests Benaiah and Jahaziel blew trumpets regularly in front of the ark of God’s covenant.{d}
On that day, for the first time, David put Asaph and his relatives in charge of singing thanks to Yahweh. This was the song:

Thank Yahweh! Pray to him by name!
Let every nation hear what he has done.{e}

Make music for him and sing his praise!
Talk about all the amazing things he does.

Be proud of his holy name!
All you who look for Yahweh, let your hearts be glad.

Turn to Yahweh and lean on his power.
Never stop seeking to be near him.

Think back on the wonders he has worked,
his miracles, and the rulings he has spoken,

you families who come from his servant Israel,
you children of Jacob, the people he chose.{f}

Yahweh is our God.
What he decides holds true in every land.

Keep his covenant in mind forever,{g}
the promise he made for a thousand generations.

He made that covenant with Abraham
and swore it to Isaac.

He made it a firm law for Jacob,
a covenant with Israel that lasts forever.

He promised, “Canaan’s land I give to you
as your own lasting share.”

At that time you were only a handful,{h}
just a few people, living as strangers there.

They wandered from one country to the next,
from one kingdom to another.

But he let no one mistreat them.
He even warned kings to leave them alone, saying,

“Keep your hands off my chosen ones!
Don’t hurt my prophets!”

Every land on earth, sing to Yahweh!{i}
Tell the good news every day that he saves.

Tell the nations how glorious he is.
Tell all peoples about his wonders.

Yahweh is great and deserves our highest praise.
Fear him more than any god.

Every god the nations worship is a useless idol,{j}
but the skies were made by Yahweh.

Splendor and greatness surround him.
Power and gladness fill his home.{k}

All you families of the earth, give Yahweh honor!
Admit that he is glorious and strong!

All the earth, shake with fear before him!
He set the world firmly in place, and it cannot be shaken.

Let the skies be happy and the earth be glad!
Let the nations be told, “Yahweh is King!”

Let the sea and all its creatures thunder!
Let the meadows and all that grows there shout for joy!

Then the forest trees will sing happily before Yahweh,
because he is coming to judge the world.

Thank Yahweh, because he is good!{m}
His faithful love goes on forever.

Pray to him, “God, our Rescuer, save us!
Bring us back together and free us from the nations.
Then we will thank your holy name
and be proud to praise you.”
Asaph and his fellow Levites stayed on, by David’s order, before the ark of Yahweh’s covenant. They were to serve there regularly, doing each day’s work as it was needed.
Obed-edom and his 68 relatives stayed to serve with them. Obed-edom, Jeduthun’s son, and Hosah kept watch as gatekeepers.{o}
David left Zadok the priest and his fellow priests in front of Yahweh’s holy tent at Gibeon’s hilltop shrine.{p}
Every morning and every evening they were to sacrifice burnt offerings to Yahweh on the altar for burnt offerings. They were to do everything written in Yahweh’s Law, which he gave to Israel.
Heman and Jeduthun were with them, along with others chosen and named for this job. They were to give thanks to Yahweh, “because his faithful love goes on forever.”{q}
Heman and Jeduthun took charge of the trumpets, the cymbals, and every instrument for the songs sung to God. Jeduthun’s sons guarded the gate.
Then the crowd broke up, and each person returned home. David, too, went back to his household to bless them.{r}

notes.text: Verses 1-3 are much like 2 Samuel 6:17-19.
The meaning of this Hebrew word is not certain. It may mean “a date cake.”
Some think the second Jeiel should be Jaaziel or Aziel, as in 15:18, 20.
Jahaziel means “God sees.”
Verses 8-22 are much like Psalm 105:1-15.
Psalm 105:6 says “you families who come from Abraham.”
Psalm 105:8 says “He has remembered his covenant forever.”
Psalm 105:12 says “when they were.”
Verses 23-33 are much like Psalm 96:1-13.
The Hebrew word for “idols” sounds like the word for “gods” and means “worthless things.”
Psalm 96:6 says “Power and beauty are in his holy place.”
Or “in the beauty of holiness.”
Verses 34-36 are much like Psalm 106:1, 47-48.
Psalm 106:48 ends, “Let all the people say, ‘Amen!’ Praise Yah!”
Jeduthun may mean “praising.” Hosah means “safe place.”
Gibeon means “hill.” Compare 21:29 and 2 Chronicles 1:3.
See 2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3; Psalms 106:1; 136:1.
2 Samuel 6:19-23 tells the same event, and also tells how Michal spoke against David.

verses.text: After David had settled into his palace, he spoke with Nathan the prophet. “Think about this,” he said. “Here I am, living in a home built of cedar wood, while the ark of Yahweh’s covenant sits under tent curtains.”{a}
Nathan answered, “Go ahead with whatever you have in mind. God is on your side.”
But that very night God gave Nathan a message.
“Go to my servant David,” God said. “Tell him that Yahweh says this: ‘You are not the man who will build me a temple to live in.{b}
I have not had a house to live in from the day I brought Israel up out of Egypt until today. My home has been a tent, carried from place to place, set up here and then there.{c}

Wherever I went with the Israelites, did I ever complain to any of their leaders? I told those leaders to care for my people like shepherds. Did I ever ask one of them, “Why haven’t you built me a temple of cedar?”’{d}
So now, tell my servant David that Yahweh of Armies says: ‘You were a shepherd boy out in the fields, walking behind the sheep, when I took you. I put you over my people Israel as their leader.
Everywhere you went, I was with you. Your enemies fell in front of you, and I swept them away. Now I will give you a great name, like the names of the mightiest men in the world.

I am choosing a homeland for my people Israel. I will plant them there like a tree, so they can live in their own place and never again be troubled. Wicked nations will not beat them down anymore, the way they used to
back in the days when I set judges over my people Israel. Every enemy of yours I will humble. And hear this: Yahweh himself will build a royal family for you.{e}
When your life is over and you go to rest with your ancestors, I will lift up a child of yours, one of your own sons, to rule after you. I will make his kingdom secure.
That son will build me a house, and I will keep his throne secure for all time.
I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.{f} My faithful love will never be pulled away from him, as I pulled it away from Saul, who ruled before you.
He will rule over my house and my kingdom without end. His throne will stand firm forever.’”{g}
Nathan told David everything God had shown him and said to him.
Then King David went in and sat down in front of Yahweh. He prayed, “Yahweh God, who am I? Why would you bring me and my family this far?
And as if that were not enough, God, you have made promises about my family’s future. Yahweh God, you have treated me as if I were a very important person.{h}
What else can I say about the honor you have given me? You know me, your servant, very well.
Yahweh, out of your own good heart and for my sake, you have done this mighty thing. You have shown me every bit of this greatness.{i}
Yahweh, no one compares with you! There is no God but you. All that we have ever heard tells us so.

Is there any other nation in the world like your people Israel? You, God, went out to free them so they could belong to you. You made your name famous by doing great and fearsome things. You chased other nations out of the way of your people, whom you rescued from Egypt.{j}
Israel became your own people for all time, and you, Yahweh, became their God.
So now, Yahweh, please keep the promise you have made about me and my family. Let it last forever. Do what you said you would do.
Then your name will stand firm and be honored forever. People will say, ‘Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, really is Israel’s God!’ And David’s dynasty will remain secure in your presence.
My God, you have opened my eyes to see that you will build a family line of kings for me. Because of that, I have dared to bring this prayer to you.
Yahweh, you alone are God! You have spoken this wonderful promise over the one who serves you.
You have been pleased to bless my family so that it will continue before you forever. When you, Yahweh, bless something, it stays blessed forever.”{k}

notes.text: Verses 1-27 are much like 2 Samuel 7:1-29. Nathan means “he has given.”
2 Samuel 7:5 asks it as a question: “Are you the one to build me a house to live in?”
The Hebrew is shortened here. Compare 2 Samuel 7:6.
The Hebrew word here is “judges.” 2 Samuel 7:7 has a similar word meaning “tribes.”
2 Samuel 7:11 says “Yahweh will make you a house.” Here “house” means a family line of kings.
Chronicles does not include the warning in 2 Samuel 7:14 about punishing him when he does wrong.
2 Samuel 7:16 says “your house and your kingdom.” Here God calls them “my house” and “my kingdom.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is not certain. Compare 2 Samuel 7:19.
2 Samuel 7:21 says “because of your promise.”
2 Samuel 7:23 adds “the nations and their gods.”
Some copies say “and may it be blessed forever.”

verses.text: Later on, David went to war with the Philistines and crushed them. He took control of Gath and the villages around it, pulling them out of Philistine hands.{a}
He beat the Moabites too. They came under David’s rule and paid him taxes every year.{b}
Next David fought Hadarezer, king of Zobah, near Hamath. Hadarezer had set out to take control of the land along the Euphrates River.{c}
David captured 1,000 of his chariots, 7,000 chariot drivers and 20,000 foot soldiers. He kept enough horses for 100 chariots. All the rest he lamed by cutting the backs of their legs.{d}
The Arameans from Damascus marched out to help Hadarezer. But David’s army killed 22,000 of them.{e}
Then David set up camps of soldiers in Aram’s land around Damascus. The Arameans came under his rule and paid him taxes. Yahweh made David win every battle, no matter where he fought.
Hadarezer’s officers carried gold shields. David took those shields back to Jerusalem.

David also took a huge amount of bronze from Tibhath and Cun, two towns Hadarezer ruled. Later Solomon used that bronze to make the big bronze tank called the Sea, the bronze pillars, and many bronze tools for the temple.{f}
King Tou of Hamath heard how David had wiped out the whole army of Hadarezer, Zobah’s king.{g}

Tou had often fought against Hadarezer. So he sent his son Hadoram to greet King David and to congratulate him on his victory. Hadoram brought gifts of every kind, made from gold, silver and bronze.{h}

King David set these gifts apart as holy, for Yahweh. He did the same with the silver and gold captured from every nation he had conquered: Edom and Moab, the Ammonites and the Philistines, and the Amalekites.
Abishai, Zeruiah’s son, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Salt Valley.{i}
He placed troops all over Edom, and the Edomites had to serve David. Wherever David went, Yahweh gave him the win.
David ruled as king over all Israel. He made sure that every one of his people was treated fairly and rightly.
Joab, Zeruiah’s son, was commander of the army. Ahilud’s son Jehoshaphat kept the royal records.{j}
Zadok, Ahitub’s son, and Abimelech, Abiathar’s son, served as priests. Shavsha was the royal writer.{k}
Benaiah, Jehoiada’s son, commanded the king’s bodyguards, the Cherethites and Pelethites. David’s sons were his chief helpers at the king’s side.{l}

notes.text: Verses 1-17 are much like 2 Samuel 8:1-18. Gath means “winepress.”
2 Samuel 8:2 also tells how many Moabite prisoners were put to death.
Hadarezer means “Hadad is help.” 2 Samuel 8:3 calls him Hadadezer. Zobah was a kingdom in Aram (Syria).
2 Samuel 8:4 says “1,700 horsemen.” Laming the horses kept them from being used in war.
The Hebrew word for “Arameans” is often translated “Syrians.” Damascus may mean “well-watered.”
2 Samuel 8:8 names the towns Betah and Berothai. Tibhath means “slaughter.” On the bronze Sea, see 2 Chronicles 4:2-5.
2 Samuel 8:9 calls him Toi.
Hadoram means “Hadad is lifted up.” 2 Samuel 8:10 calls him Joram, “Yahweh is lifted up.”
2 Samuel 8:13 gives David the credit. The heading of Psalm 60 says Joab killed 12,000. Edom means “red.”
Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.” Ahilud means “a brother is born.”
Many copies, and 2 Samuel 8:17, say “Ahimelech son of Abiathar.” 2 Samuel 8:17 also calls the writer Seraiah. Abimelech means “my father is king.”
2 Samuel 8:18 says “David’s sons were priests.” The Cherethites and Pelethites were foreign guards, perhaps from Crete and Philistia.

verses.text: Later, the Ammonite ruler Nahash passed away, and his son Hanun was crowned in his place.{a}

David thought, “Nahash treated me kindly. Now I will show the same kindness to Hanun.” So David sent some officials to tell Hanun how sorry he was about his father’s death. They arrived in the land of Ammon to comfort Hanun.{b}

But Hanun’s own princes warned him, “You think David is showing respect for your father by sending comforters? Not at all! These men are spies. He sent them to look over our land so he can attack it and destroy it.”
So Hanun grabbed David’s officials. He shaved their faces bare and chopped their robes short at the waist, so their bodies showed. Then he sent them away.

When David learned how his men had been treated, he sent people to meet them, because they were so ashamed. The king’s message was, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back. Then you may come home.”{c}

The Ammonites knew that they had made David their bitter enemy. So Hanun and the Ammonites paid out about 37 tons of silver{d} to rent chariots and chariot drivers from northwest Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah.{e}

With that money they hired 32,000 chariots. The king of Maacah also came with his army, and they set up camp close to Medeba. Meanwhile the Ammonites gathered from their towns and got ready to fight.{f}
David heard about it. He sent out Joab with Israel’s whole army of fighting men.
The Ammonites marched out and lined up for battle by the gate of their city. The kings who had come to help stayed apart from them, out in the open country.
Joab saw that enemy lines faced him both in front and behind. So he picked the very best of Israel’s soldiers and sent them to fight the Arameans.
The remaining soldiers he placed under the command of Abishai, his brother. Abishai lined them up opposite the Ammonites.
Joab told him, “If the Arameans are beating me, come and rescue me. If the Ammonites are beating you, I’ll come and rescue you.
Take heart! Let’s fight bravely for our people and for the cities that belong to our God. May Yahweh do whatever seems good to him.”
Joab and his troops advanced to attack the Arameans. And the Arameans fled from him.
Seeing the Arameans flee, the Ammonites also ran from Abishai, Joab’s brother, and hurried back inside their city. Then Joab went home to Jerusalem.
The Arameans knew Israel had beaten them. So they sent messengers to bring more Arameans from across the Euphrates River. At their head marched Shophach, who commanded Hadarezer’s forces.{g}
When David got the news, he gathered all Israel’s troops. They crossed the Jordan River and marched straight up to the Arameans. David set his army in position, and the Arameans attacked.
But the Arameans were driven back by Israel and ran away. David’s soldiers killed 7,000 of their chariot drivers and 40,000 of their foot soldiers. They also killed Shophach, the army commander.{h}
Hadarezer’s officers knew they had lost to Israel. They asked David for peace and became his servants. After that, the Arameans refused to help the Ammonites ever again.

notes.text: Verses 1-19 are much like 2 Samuel 10:1-19. Nahash means “snake.” Ammon means “people.”
Hanun means “favored.”
Jericho may mean “moon city.”
The Hebrew says “1,000 talents.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds.
The Hebrew says Aram-naharaim, meaning “Aram of the two rivers.” 2 Samuel 10:6 names Beth-rehob, Zobah, Maacah and Tob.
2 Samuel 10:6 says 20,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 men from Tob. Medeba may mean “quiet waters.”
2 Samuel 10:16 calls him Shobach.
2 Samuel 10:18 says the men of 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen.

verses.text: The next spring, at the season when kings usually march off to battle, Joab took the army out and laid waste the Ammonites’ country. He surrounded the city of Rabbah and cut it off, while David remained in Jerusalem. Joab struck Rabbah and left it in ruins.{a}

David lifted the crown off the head of their king.{b} It was made of gold, weighed about 75 pounds,{c} and held valuable jewels. Then the crown was placed on David’s head. He also carried away a great load of riches from the city.

He made the people of the city come out and set them to hard work with saws, iron picks and axes.{d} Every Ammonite town got the same treatment from David. Afterward he and all his troops went back to Jerusalem.
Later, fighting broke out with the Philistines at Gezer. There Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who came from the race of giants.{e} So the Philistines were beaten down.
War with the Philistines flared up once more. This time Jair’s son Elhanan killed Lahmi, Goliath’s brother. Goliath came from Gath, and his spear handle was as thick as the bar of a weaving loom.{f}
Yet another battle took place at Gath. There was a huge man there who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He too came from the giants’ family line.{g}
This man made fun of Israel. So Jonathan, whose father Shimea was David’s brother, killed him.{h}
These giants came from Gath. David and his soldiers killed every one of them.

notes.text: Verses 1-3 are much like 2 Samuel 11:1; 12:26, 30-31. Chronicles does not tell the story of Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11:2-12:25). Rabbah means “great city.”
Or “the crown of Milcom,” the Ammonite god. The Hebrew letters can be read either way.
The Hebrew says “a talent.”
The Hebrew word here can mean “he sawed them,” but it is probably a copying mistake for “he set them to work.” Compare 2 Samuel 12:31.
The Hebrew says “the Rephaim,” a people known for being very tall. 2 Samuel 21:18 has “Saph” and “at Gob.”

2 Samuel 21:19 says “Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim of Bethlehem killed Goliath of Gath.” Chronicles names the giant Lahmi and calls him Goliath’s brother (compare 1 Samuel 17). Jair means “he gives light.”
Verses 6-8 are much like 2 Samuel 21:20-22.
Shimea means “heard.”

verses.text: Satan rose up to attack Israel. He stirred up David to take a count of the Israelites.{a}
So David gave an order to Joab and the army leaders. “Travel the whole land, from Beersheba up to Dan, and number Israel,” he said. “Bring the total back to me. I want to learn how large it is.”{b}

Joab objected. “May Yahweh make his people grow a hundred times larger than they are now! Your Majesty, every one of them already serves you. What is your reason for this? It will only make Israel guilty.”
Still, the king would not change his mind, and Joab had to give in. So Joab left and traveled all over Israel. Then he came back to Jerusalem.
He gave David the totals. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who could fight with swords. In Judah there were 470,000.{c}
But Joab left out the tribes of Levi and Benjamin, because he hated the king’s order.{d}
God was not pleased with what David had done, so he punished Israel.
Then David prayed to God, “What I did was a great sin. Please forgive me, your servant. I have been a complete fool.”
Yahweh gave a message to Gad, the prophet who served David.{e}
“Go and tell David that Yahweh says this,” God said. “‘I am giving you three choices. Pick one, and I will do it to you.’”
Gad went to David and told him, “Yahweh says, ‘Make your choice.

You may have three years without enough food. Or you may run from your enemies for three months, while their swords catch up with you. Or you may have three days of Yahweh’s own sword. That would be a terrible sickness spreading through the land, with Yahweh’s angel bringing death everywhere in Israel.’ Now think it over. What answer should I take back to the One who sent me?”{f}
“I am in deep trouble,” David answered. “Let me fall into Yahweh’s hands, because his mercy is very great. Don’t let me fall into human hands.”
So Yahweh sent a deadly sickness on Israel, and 70,000 Israelite men died.

God also sent an angel toward Jerusalem to wipe it out. But the moment the angel began, Yahweh saw it and felt sorry about the suffering. “Stop! It is enough,” he told the destroying angel. “Lower your hand.” At that moment the angel of Yahweh stood beside the threshing floor of Ornan, a Jebusite man.{g}

David looked up and saw the angel of Yahweh standing in the air between the earth and the sky. The angel held a sword in his hand, reaching out over Jerusalem. Then David and the leaders, all dressed in rough cloth to show their sorrow, bowed with their faces to the ground.{h}

David cried out to God, “I’m the one who gave the order to count the people! I’m the one who sinned and did evil. These people are like innocent sheep. What did they ever do? Yahweh my God, punish me and my family, not your people. Stop this sickness from killing them.”
Then the angel of Yahweh told Gad to give David a message. David was to go up to Ornan’s threshing floor and build an altar to Yahweh there.
So David went, just as Gad had told him to do in Yahweh’s name.
Ornan was busy threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him ran and hid.{i}
Then David came toward Ornan. When Ornan saw him, he left the threshing floor and bowed down low in front of David with his face touching the ground.

“Sell me this spot where you thresh grain,” David told him, “so that I may put up an altar for Yahweh here. I will pay you everything it is worth. Then the sickness that is killing the people will stop.”

Ornan told David, “It’s yours, my lord the king! Do whatever you think is best. Look, I’ll give you the oxen for the burnt offerings. Here are the wooden threshing boards to burn, and the wheat for the grain offering. I’m giving you all of it.”
King David refused. “No, I must pay you all that it’s worth. I won’t take something that belongs to you and give it to Yahweh. I won’t offer him a burnt offering that cost me nothing.”
For the site, David handed Ornan gold weighing about 15 pounds.{j}

David built an altar to Yahweh there. He sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on Yahweh. Yahweh answered him by sending fire down from heaven onto the altar for burnt offerings.{k}
Then Yahweh gave the angel an order, and the angel slid his sword back into its holder.
David saw that Yahweh had answered his prayer at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. So from then on he offered sacrifices there.
At that time Yahweh’s holy tent, which Moses had made in the desert, stood on the hilltop shrine at Gibeon, along with the altar for burnt offerings.
But David could not go there to ask God what to do. He was too frightened of the sword of Yahweh’s angel.

notes.text: Verses 1-27 are much like 2 Samuel 24:1-25. 2 Samuel 24:1 says Yahweh was angry with Israel and stirred David against them. The Hebrew word satan can be a name or can mean “an enemy.”
Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the promise.” Dan means “judge.”
2 Samuel 24:9 gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. The two counts may have been taken in different ways.
Compare Numbers 1:47-49.
Gad means “good fortune.”
2 Samuel 24:13 says “seven years.” The Septuagint of Samuel says “three years,” as here.
Ornan is called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24:16. The name may mean “lord.”
An old Dead Sea Scroll copy of 2 Samuel has a verse like this at 2 Samuel 24:16. Rough cloth here is sackcloth, worn when people mourned.
2 Samuel 24:20 says only that Araunah saw the king and his officials coming.

The Hebrew says “600 shekels of gold.” 2 Samuel 24:24 says David paid 50 shekels of silver, about 1 1/4 pounds, for the threshing floor and the oxen. Chronicles speaks of the whole site where the temple would later stand.
See Leviticus 9:24 and 1 Kings 18:38.

verses.text: Then David announced, “Right here is where the house of Yahweh God will stand. Here is where Israel’s altar for burnt offerings will be.”{a}
David gave orders to bring together all the foreigners living in Israel. He put some of them to work as stonecutters, shaping blocks of stone for building God’s house.
He stored up large amounts of iron to make nails and hinges for the gate doors. He also stored up so much bronze that no one could weigh it all,
and cedar beams past counting, since boatloads of cedar kept arriving for David from Sidon and Tyre.{b}

David said to himself, “My son Solomon is young and has little experience. But the house we build for Yahweh must be wonderful beyond words. It must be famous and admired in every land. So I will get everything ready for it now.” That is why David made such huge preparations before he died.
Then David sent for his son Solomon. He gave him the job of building a house for Yahweh, Israel’s God.
“My son,” David told Solomon, “I wanted with all my heart to build a temple to honor the name of Yahweh my God.
But Yahweh told me, ‘You have killed many people and fought many great wars. Because of all the blood I have watched you spill on the earth, the house for my name will not be built by you.

Instead, a son will be born to you who will live in calm and rest. I will keep his enemies around him from troubling him. Solomon will be his name, and during his reign I will grant Israel peace and quiet.{c}
That son will build a house for my name. I will treat him as my own child, and he will have me as his Father. I will make his royal throne over Israel last forever.’
Now, my son, I pray that Yahweh will be with you. I pray that you will succeed and build the house of Yahweh your God, just as he said you would.
May Yahweh give you good sense and understanding when he puts you in charge of Israel. Then you will obey the teaching of Yahweh your God.
If you carefully follow the rules and laws Yahweh gave Moses for Israel, you will succeed. Be brave and strong! Don’t be afraid, and don’t lose heart.

Look, I have worked hard to get things ready for Yahweh’s house. I have put aside gold, about 3,750 tons of it, and silver, about 37,500 tons.{d} The bronze and iron are too heavy to weigh. I have stored up wood and stone too, and you can add more.
You have plenty of workers: men who cut stone, men who build with stone and wood, and experts in every kind of skill.
You have more gold, silver, bronze and iron than anyone can count. So get started, and may Yahweh be with you!”
Next, David commanded every leader in Israel to give Solomon their help.

“Isn’t Yahweh your God beside you?” he asked. “All around you, he has brought rest from war. He let me defeat the people who lived in this land. Now the land lies conquered before Yahweh and his people.

So now, give your whole heart and soul to following Yahweh your God. Get to work and build the holy place of Yahweh God. Then bring in the ark of Yahweh’s covenant and the holy objects that belong to God. Put them in the house built to honor Yahweh’s name.”

notes.text: This verse names Ornan’s threshing floor as the place for the temple. Compare 2 Chronicles 3:1.
Sidon means “fishing.” Tyre means “rock.”
The Hebrew name Solomon, Shelomoh, sounds like shalom, the word for “peace.”
The Hebrew says “100,000 talents of gold and 1,000,000 talents of silver.” These numbers are huge and may be meant to show how much there was. Compare 29:4, 7.

subheads.2: David Prepares to Build the Temple

verses.text: When David had grown very old and had lived a long, full life, he put his son Solomon on the throne as Israel’s king.{a}
He called together all of Israel’s leaders, along with the priests and the Levites.
Every Levite man aged thirty or more was counted one by one. There were 38,000 in all.{b}
David said, “Out of these, 24,000 will direct the work at Yahweh’s house. Six thousand more will act as officers and as judges for the people.
Gate duty will go to 4,000 of them. The last 4,000 will praise Yahweh, playing the instruments I have made for worship.”{c}
David split the Levites into groups following the families of Levi’s three sons, Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
From Gershon came the families of Ladan and Shimei.{d}
Ladan had three sons. Jehiel was the oldest, then came Zetham and Joel.{e}
From Shimei came three sons, Shelomoth, Haziel and Haran. Each of these men led one of Ladan’s family groups.{f}
Shimei also had four other sons: Jahath, Zina, Jeush and Beriah.{g}
Jahath was first, and Zizah was second. Since Jeush and Beriah had only a few sons, their two families were joined and given a single task.{h}
Born to Kohath were four boys: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel.

Two sons were born to Amram, Aaron and Moses. Aaron and his descendants were set apart for all time to care for the most holy things. They were to burn incense to Yahweh, to serve him, and to speak blessings in his name forever.
Moses was a man of God, yet his sons were simply listed with the rest of Levi’s tribe.
Moses had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer.
Shebuel was the leader of Gershom’s descendants.{i}
Rehabiah was the leader of Eliezer’s descendants. Eliezer had no other sons, but Rehabiah had a great many.{j}
Shelomith led the family of Izhar.{k}
In Hebron’s family, Jeriah was the head. After him came Amariah, then Jahaziel, then Jekameam.{l}
In Uzziel’s family, Micah was first and Isshiah was second.{m}
Merari had two sons, Mahli and Mushi. Mahli’s two sons were Eleazar and Kish.
When Eleazar died, he left only daughters and no sons. They married their cousins, Kish’s sons.
Mushi had three sons: Mahli, Eder and Jeremoth.{n}

Those were the descendants of Levi, listed by families. They were the family leaders, with each name counted and written down. Every one of them, aged twenty and up, worked to serve at Yahweh’s house.{o}
David had said, “Yahweh, Israel’s God, has given his people rest. Jerusalem will be his home for all time.
So the Levites won’t have to carry the holy tent or the things used in its worship anymore.”
Following David’s final instructions, the Levites aged twenty and older were counted.

Their job was to help Aaron’s descendants as they served at Yahweh’s house. They took care of the courtyards and side rooms, kept all the holy things clean, and did any other work needed at God’s house.

They were in charge of the holy bread set out in rows, the fine flour for grain offerings, and the thin bread made without yeast. They took care of the baked offerings and the offerings mixed with oil. They also checked every measure of amount and size.
Each morning they stood up to thank and praise Yahweh, and they did the same again each evening.
They helped whenever burnt offerings were brought to Yahweh on Sabbath days, at the new moon celebrations, and at the other feasts. A set number of them served before Yahweh at all times.
So they took care of the tent where God met his people and the holy place. They also assisted Aaron’s family, their own relatives, in the work of Yahweh’s house.

notes.text: Compare 1 Kings 1:1-40, which tells about a struggle over who would be king. Chronicles does not tell that story.

Numbers 4:3 sets the starting age at thirty, and Numbers 8:24 at twenty-five. Verses 24 and 27 say twenty, as in 2 Chronicles 31:17 and Ezra 3:8. Verse 27 explains that David made this change near the end of his life.
The Septuagint says “that he made.”
Ladan is called Libni in 6:17 and Exodus 6:17.
Zetham means “olive tree.”
Some think this Shimei should be Jehiel, since Shimei’s sons are listed in verse 10. Shelomoth means “peaceful.” Haziel means “God sees.”
Zina is called Zizah in verse 11.
Or “one group for duty.”
Shebuel, called Shubael in 24:20, may mean “come back, O God.”
Rehabiah means “Yahweh has made room.”
Shelomith is called Shelomoth in 24:22.
Jeriah means “Yahweh sees.” Jekameam means “may the people rise.”
Isshiah means “Yahweh lends.”
Eder means “flock.”
See the note on verse 3.

verses.text: Aaron’s descendants were sorted into work groups in this way. Four sons were born to Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.{a}
The first two sons died before their father did, leaving no children behind. That left Eleazar and Ithamar to serve as priests.{b}
David divided the priests into groups for their turns of duty. Zadok, from Eleazar’s line, and Ahimelech, from Ithamar’s line, helped him.{c}
Eleazar’s family had more leaders than Ithamar’s. So they were divided like this: sixteen family leaders from Eleazar’s side and eight from Ithamar’s side.
They used lots to divide both families fairly. That was because officials of the holy place and officials of God came from both Eleazar’s and Ithamar’s descendants.

The Levite Shemaiah, son of Nethanel, was the writer who wrote down their names. The king and his officials watched, along with Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the priest and Levite families. One family was picked from Eleazar’s side, then one from Ithamar’s side, taking turns.{d}
The first lot fell to Jehoiarib. The second fell to Jedaiah,{e}
the third to Harim, and the fourth to Seorim.{f}
Fifth came Malchijah, and sixth Mijamin.{g}
Seventh came Hakkoz, and eighth Abijah.{h}
Ninth came Jeshua, and tenth Shecaniah.{i}
Eleventh came Eliashib, and twelfth Jakim.{j}
Thirteenth came Huppah, and fourteenth Jeshebeab.{k}
Fifteenth came Bilgah, and sixteenth Immer.{l}
Seventeenth came Hezir, and eighteenth Happizzez.{m}
Nineteenth came Pethahiah, and twentieth Jehezkel.{n}
Twenty-first came Jachin, and twenty-second Gamul.{o}
Twenty-third came Delaiah, and twenty-fourth Maaziah.{p}
This was the order in which they took turns going into Yahweh’s house to serve. They followed the rules their ancestor Aaron had given them, just as Yahweh, Israel’s God, had told him.
Here are the rest of Levi’s descendants. From Amram’s line came Shubael, and from Shubael’s line, Jehdeiah.{q}
Rehabiah’s line was led by Isshiah, the oldest.
From Izhar’s line came Shelomoth, and from Shelomoth’s line, Jahath.
Hebron’s line:{r} Jeriah was the head, then Amariah, then Jahaziel, and then Jekameam.
From Uzziel’s line came Micah, and from Micah’s line, Shamir.{s}
Micah had a brother, Isshiah, and from Isshiah’s line came Zechariah.
Merari’s descendants were Mahli and Mushi. From Jaaziah came Beno.{t}
Merari’s descendants through Jaaziah were Beno, Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri.{u}
From Mahli came Eleazar, who had no sons.
From Kish came Jerahmeel.{v}
Born to Mushi were Mahli, Eder and Jerimoth. All of these were Levites, listed by families.

Just like their relatives, Aaron’s descendants, these Levites also drew lots to assign their duties. King David watched, along with Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the priest and Levite families. The oldest brother’s family was treated the same as the youngest brother’s.

notes.text: Abihu means “he is my father.” Ithamar may mean “island of palms.”
See Leviticus 10:1-2.
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.”
The Hebrew here is hard to read. The Septuagint says “one for Eleazar, and one for Ithamar.” Nethanel means “God has given.”
Jehoiarib means “Yahweh argues the case.” Many years later, the Maccabee family belonged to this group (1 Maccabees 2:1).
Harim means “set apart.” Seorim means “barley.”
Mijamin means “from the right hand.”
Hakkoz means “the thorn.” Abijah means “Yahweh is father.” Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, belonged to Abijah’s group (Luke 1:5).
Jeshua means “Yahweh saves.” Shecaniah means “Yahweh has lived among us.”
Eliashib means “God brings back.”
Huppah means “canopy.” Jeshebeab may mean “father’s home.”
Bilgah means “cheerful.”
Hezir means “pig.” Happizzez means “the breaking.”
Pethahiah means “Yahweh opens.” Jehezkel, the same name as Ezekiel, means “God makes strong.”
Gamul means “weaned.”
Delaiah means “Yahweh has drawn up.” Maaziah means “Yahweh is a safe place.”
Jehdeiah means “Yahweh is glad.”
The words “Hebron’s line” come from 23:19. The Hebrew says “And my sons.”
Some Hebrew copies say Shamur. Shamir means “thorn.”
The Hebrew of verses 26-27 is unclear. Beno may be a name, or it may mean “his son.” Jaaziah means “Yahweh makes strong.”
Shoham means “onyx.” Zaccur means “remembered.” Ibri means “Hebrew.”
Jerahmeel means “God shows mercy.”

verses.text: David and the army leaders also chose some of the descendants of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun for special service. They were to speak God’s messages as they played lyres, harps and cymbals. Here are the men who did this work:{a}
From Asaph’s family came Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah and Asharelah. Their father Asaph directed them, and he spoke God’s messages whenever the king ordered.{b}

From Jeduthun’s family came six sons: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei,{c} Hashabiah and Mattithiah. Their father Jeduthun directed them. He played the lyre and spoke God’s messages as he thanked and praised Yahweh.{d}
From Heman’s family came Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, as well as Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti and Romamti-ezer, and also Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir and Mahazioth.{e}

Every one of these was a son of Heman, who served the king as a seer. Through God’s promises, Heman was to be lifted high in honor.{f} So God blessed him with a family of fourteen boys and three girls.

Their fathers directed all of them as they made music at Yahweh’s house. They played cymbals, harps and lyres as part of the worship at God’s house. The king himself was in charge of Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman.
Together with their relatives, these men were trained and skilled at making music for Yahweh. There were 288 of them in all.
Young and old, teachers and students, all drew lots to decide their turns of duty.
Lot one, for Asaph’s family, went to Joseph.{g} Lot two went to Gedaliah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot three went to Zaccur. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot four went to Izri.{h} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot five went to Nethaniah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot six went to Bukkiah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot seven went to Jesharelah.{i} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot eight went to Jeshaiah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot nine went to Mattaniah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot ten went to Shimei. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot eleven went to Azarel.{j} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twelve went to Hashabiah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot thirteen went to Shubael.{k} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot fourteen went to Mattithiah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot fifteen went to Jeremoth.{l} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot sixteen went to Hananiah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot seventeen went to Joshbekashah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot eighteen went to Hanani. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot nineteen went to Mallothi. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twenty went to Eliathah. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twenty-one went to Hothir. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twenty-two went to Giddalti. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twenty-three went to Mahazioth. His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.
Lot twenty-four went to Romamti-ezer.{m} His group of sons and relatives numbered 12.

notes.text: On Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, see 6:33, 39 and 16:41. Here their music is called prophecy (compare 2 Kings 3:15).
Joseph means “may he add.” Nethaniah means “Yahweh has given.” Asharelah, called Jesharelah in verse 14, may mean “honest toward God.”
The name Shimei comes from verse 17. The Hebrew lists only five names but says “six.”
Gedaliah means “Yahweh is great.” Zeri, called Izri in verse 11, may mean “healing oil.” Jeshaiah means “Yahweh saves.”

Bukkiah means “Yahweh’s jar.” Shebuel is called Shubael in verse 20, and Jerimoth is called Jeremoth in verse 22. Hananiah means “Yahweh is kind.” Read together, the last names in this verse sound like a short prayer in Hebrew: “Be kind to me, Yah, be kind to me. You are my God. I have made great and lifted high your help. Sitting in trouble, I have spoken. He has given many visions.”
The Hebrew says “to lift up his horn,” a way of saying “to give strength or honor.”
The Hebrew gives no number for Joseph’s group. The total of 288 (verse 7) means each of the 24 groups had 12.
Izri is called Zeri in verse 3.
Jesharelah is called Asharelah in verse 2.
Azarel is called Uzziel in verse 4. Azarel means “God helps.”
Shubael is called Shebuel in verse 4.
Jeremoth is called Jerimoth in verse 4.
The 24 groups of musicians match the 24 groups of priests in chapter 24.

verses.text: Here are the groups of gatekeepers. From Korah’s family came Meshelemiah, Kore’s son, one of Asaph’s descendants.{a}
Meshelemiah’s oldest son was Zechariah. Jediael came second, Zebadiah third, Jathniel fourth,{b}
Elam fifth, Jehohanan sixth and Eliehoenai seventh.{c}
Obed-edom’s oldest son was Shemaiah. Jehozabad came second, Joah third, Sachar fourth, Nethanel fifth,{d}
Ammiel sixth, Issachar seventh and Peullethai eighth. God had truly blessed Obed-edom.{e}
Shemaiah, Obed-edom’s son, became the father of sons who rose to lead their family, because they were very able men.
Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad were born to Shemaiah. Two relatives of theirs, Elihu and Semachiah, were strong men too.{f}
Every one of these came from Obed-edom’s family. Together with their sons and relatives, they were capable men, strong enough for the work. Obed-edom’s family had 62 of them.
Meshelemiah’s family had 18 sons and relatives, all of them capable men.
Hosah, from Merari’s family, had sons too. Shimri was made the leader. He was not the oldest, but his father put him in charge.{g}
Hilkiah came second, Tebaliah third and Zechariah fourth. Hosah’s sons and relatives numbered 13 in all.{h}
These groups of gatekeepers, led by their chief men, had duties at Yahweh’s house, just as their relatives did.
Family by family, they drew lots to decide which gate each would guard. Small families and large ones were treated alike.
Shelemiah won the lot for the East Gate. Then they drew lots for his son Zechariah, a man who gave wise advice, and he got the North Gate.{i}
Obed-edom drew the South Gate, and his sons drew the storehouse.{j}
Shuppim and Hosah got the West Gate and the Shallecheth Gate on the road that climbs the hill. The guards took turns, one after another.{k}
Each day six Levites kept watch on the east side, while four stood guard to the north and four more to the south. Two at a time watched each storehouse.
At the courtyard on the west side, four guarded the road and two guarded the courtyard.{l}
These were the groups of gatekeepers who came from the families of Korah and Merari.
Other Levites, led by Ahijah, took charge of the treasure rooms of God’s house and the rooms where gifts given to God were stored.{m}
Ladan was a Gershonite, and his descendants led families. Jehieli was one of these leaders.{n}
Jehieli’s sons, Zetham and his brother Joel, looked after the treasure rooms of Yahweh’s house.
Other leaders came from the families of Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel.
Shebuel, a descendant of Moses’ son Gershom, was the chief officer over the treasure rooms.
His relatives came through Eliezer. Eliezer’s son was Rehabiah, and after him came Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and Shelomoth.{o}

Shelomoth and his relatives took care of all the treasures set apart for God. These had been given by King David, the family leaders, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the other army officers.{p}
From the things they had captured in battle, they gave some to God to help repair and keep up Yahweh’s house.

Shelomoth and his relatives also cared for everything given to God by Samuel the seer, by Saul, the son of Kish, and by Ner’s son Abner and Zeruiah’s son Joab. All the holy gifts were in their care.{q}
From Izhar’s family, Chenaniah and his sons were given work away from the temple. They served Israel as officers and judges.{r}

From Hebron’s family, Hashabiah and 1,700 of his relatives, all capable men, were given oversight of the Israelites living on the western side of the Jordan River. They handled all of Yahweh’s work there and also the king’s business.{s}

Jerijah was the leader of Hebron’s family, according to their family records. In the fortieth year that David was king, a search was made in the records. Strong, able men from Hebron’s family were found living at Jazer in Gilead.{t}

Jerijah had 2,700 relatives who were capable men and family leaders. King David gave them authority over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the people of East Manasseh. They took care of everything that had to do with God and with the king.

notes.text: Meshelemiah, called Shelemiah in verse 14, means “Yahweh pays back.” “Asaph” may be a copying mistake for Ebiasaph (9:19).
Jathniel means “God gives.”
Jehohanan means “Yahweh is kind.” Eliehoenai means “my eyes look to Yahweh.”
Jehozabad means “Yahweh has given.” Sachar means “reward.”
Ammiel means “God is my relative.” Peullethai means “Yahweh’s payment.” Compare 13:14.
Othni may mean “my strength.” Rephael means “God heals.” Semachiah means “Yahweh holds up.”
Shimri means “Yahweh guards.”
Tebaliah means “Yahweh has dipped.”
Shelemiah is the same man as Meshelemiah in verse 1.
The Hebrew says “house of gatherings.”
The name Shuppim may be a copying mistake repeating the last Hebrew word of verse 15. Shallecheth means “throwing out.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “courtyard,” parbar, is not certain. It may mean a porch with columns.
The Septuagint says “their relatives” instead of “Ahijah.”
Jehieli is a family name that comes from Jehiel (23:8).
Joram means “Yahweh is lifted up.”
Some Hebrew copies spell the name Shelomith.
Abner means “father of light.” Samuel may mean “name of God” or “heard by God.”
Chenaniah means “Yahweh makes firm.”
The Hebrew says “beyond the Jordan westward,” that is, west of the Jordan.
Jerijah, called Jeriah in 23:19, means “Yahweh sees.” Jazer means “he helps.”

verses.text: Below are the Israelites who served the king: family heads, leaders over units of a thousand or a hundred, and their officers. They were in charge of the army groups that took turns on duty, one group each month all year long. Every group had 24,000 men.{a}
Jashobeam, Zabdiel’s son, led the group on duty in the first month, March to April. His group had 24,000 men.{b}
He came from Perez’s family. He was chief over all the army officers who served that first month.
Dodai from Ahoah led the group for the second month, April to May. Mikloth was its chief officer. That group also had 24,000 men.{c}
Benaiah led the group for the third month, May to June. His father was Jehoiada, the chief priest. Benaiah’s group had 24,000 men.{d}
Benaiah was a mighty fighter, one of the Thirty, and he commanded them. His son Ammizabad was in charge of his group.{e}
Asahel, Joab’s brother, led the group for the fourth month, June to July. His son Zebadiah took his place after him. There were 24,000 in his group.{f}
Shamhuth from Izrah led the group for the fifth month, July to August. He had 24,000 men.{g}
For the sixth month, August to September, the leader was Ira, Ikkesh’s son, from Tekoa. He had 24,000 men.
For the seventh month, September to October, the leader was Helez from Pelon, of Ephraim’s tribe. He had 24,000 men.
For the eighth month, October to November, the leader was Sibbecai from Hushah, of Zerah’s family. He had 24,000 men.{h}
For the ninth month, November to December, the leader was Abiezer from Anathoth, of Benjamin’s tribe. He had 24,000 men.
For the tenth month, December to January, the leader was Maharai from Netophah, of Zerah’s family. He had 24,000 men.
For the eleventh month, January to February, the leader was Benaiah from Pirathon, of Ephraim’s tribe. He had 24,000 men.
For the twelfth month, February to March, the leader was Heldai from Netophah, of Othniel’s family. He had 24,000 men.{i}
These men were the officers over Israel’s tribes. Zichri’s son Eliezer led Reuben. Maacah’s son Shephatiah led Simeon.{j}
Kemuel’s son Hashabiah led Levi. Zadok led Aaron’s family.{k}
Elihu, one of David’s brothers, led Judah. Michael’s son Omri led Issachar.{l}
Obadiah’s son Ishmaiah led Zebulun. Azriel’s son Jerimoth led Naphtali.{m}
Azaziah’s son Hoshea led Ephraim. Pedaiah’s son Joel led the western half of Manasseh.{n}
Zechariah’s son Iddo led the half of Manasseh living in Gilead. Abner’s son Jaasiel led Benjamin.{o}
Jeroham’s son Azarel led Dan. These were the officers in charge of Israel’s tribes.{p}
David left out everyone younger than twenty when he counted the people. That was because Yahweh had promised to multiply Israel until they were like the countless stars overhead.
Joab, Zeruiah’s son, began counting but stopped before he was done. Because of that count, God’s anger fell on Israel. So the total was never written in King David’s official history book.{q}
Azmaveth son of Adiel was in charge of the king’s treasure rooms. Jonathan son of Uzziah managed the storehouses out in the country, in the towns, in the villages and in the watchtowers.{r}
Ezri son of Chelub managed the field workers who plowed the land.{s}
Shimei from Ramah took care of the vineyards. Zabdi from Shepham took care of the wine from the vineyards that was kept in the cellars.{t}
Baal-hanan, a man of Geder, oversaw the olive groves and the fig orchards in the low western hills. Joash was over the stores of olive oil.{u}
Shitrai from Sharon looked after the cattle that grazed on the Sharon plain. Adlai’s son Shaphat looked after the cattle in the valleys.{v}
Obil, an Ishmaelite, cared for the camels. Jehdeiah from Meronoth cared for the female donkeys.{w}
Jaziz, a Hagrite, cared for the sheep and goats. All these men managed the property that belonged to King David.{x}
David’s uncle Jonathan was a wise adviser and a writer who understood things well. Hachmoni’s son Jehiel helped bring up the king’s sons.{y}
Ahithophel gave advice to the king, and Hushai from the Arkite clan was the king’s close friend.{z}
When Ahithophel was gone, Jehoiada son of Benaiah and Abiathar took his place as advisers. Joab commanded the king’s army.{aa}

notes.text: The months in this chapter are counted from the new year in spring. The Hebrew says “the first month,” “the second month,” and so on. Because the months followed the moon, each one covers parts of two of our months.
Zabdiel means “gift of God.” Perez means “breaking out.”
The Hebrew is unclear here. It may mean “Eleazar, son of Dodai” (11:12). Dodai means “loved one.”
Or “Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the chief.”
Ammizabad means “my people has given.”
Abner killed Asahel before David ruled all Israel (2 Samuel 2:23). So his son Zebadiah may have held this job in his father’s name.
Shamhuth may mean “ruin.” He may be the Shammoth of 11:27.
The Zerahites came from Zerah, Judah’s son (2:4).
Heldai, called Heled in 11:30, may mean “mole.” Othniel may mean “God is my strength.”
Gad and Asher are not listed. Levi and Aaron are counted separately.
Kemuel means “God raises up.”
The Septuagint says Eliab, David’s oldest brother (2:13).
Ishmaiah means “Yahweh hears.” Azriel means “God is my help.”
Hoshea means “rescue.” Pedaiah means “Yahweh has set free.”
Iddo may mean “on time.” Jaasiel means “God makes.”
Azarel means “God helps.”
See chapter 21. The Hebrew says “the record of the days of King David.”
Adiel means “ornament of God.” Uzziah means “Yahweh is strength.”
Ezri means “my help.”
Ramah means “height.” Shepham may be the place named in Numbers 34:10.
The Hebrew says “the Shephelah,” meaning “lowland.” These were the low hills west of Judah. Baal-hanan means “the Lord is kind.” The fig trees were sycamore figs.
Sharon means “plain.” Shitrai may mean “officer.”
Obil means “camel driver.” The Ishmaelites came from Ishmael, whose name means “God hears.”
Jaziz may mean “he moves.” The Hagrites were a desert people (5:10).
The Hebrew word for “uncle” can also mean “relative” or “loved one.” Hachmoni means “wise.”
Ahithophel means “brother of foolishness.” Hushai means “quick.” See 2 Samuel 15:12, 32-37.
Joab means “Yahweh is father.”

verses.text: David ordered all of Israel’s leaders to gather in Jerusalem. He called the heads of the tribes and the commanders of the army groups that served the king. He called the commanders of thousands and of hundreds and the men who managed all the land and animals owned by the king and his sons. He also called the palace officials, the heroes and all the brave soldiers.

King David rose to his feet and spoke. “Hear what I have to say, my brothers, my people,” he began. “I truly wanted to build a house where the ark of Yahweh’s covenant could rest. It would be a footstool for our God. I got everything ready to build it.{a}
God, however, told me, ‘A house for my name is not a job for you. You have been a soldier, and you have killed people.’

Even so, Yahweh, Israel’s God, picked me out of my whole family to rule Israel forever. First he chose Judah to lead. From Judah’s clans he picked out my father’s household. And out of my father’s sons, he was glad to make me king of all Israel.
Yahweh has given me a great many sons. Out of them all, he picked my son Solomon to sit on the throne of Yahweh’s kingdom and rule Israel.{b}
Yahweh told me, ‘It will be Solomon, your son, who builds my house and its courtyards. I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his Father.
If he keeps on obeying my commands and laws as carefully as he does now, his kingdom will stand firm for all time.’

So now, while all Israel, Yahweh’s people, watches, and while our God listens, I tell you this: Be careful to obey every command of Yahweh your God. Then this good land will stay yours, and you can hand it down to your children after you forever.

“Solomon, my son, come to know the God your father has served. Give yourself to serving him gladly, holding nothing back. Yahweh looks deep into every heart. He knows every plan and every thought. Search for him, and he will let himself be found by you. Leave him, and he will throw you off for good.
Pay attention! Yahweh has chosen you to build a house to be his holy place. Be strong and get it done.”

Then David handed his son Solomon the plans for the temple. They showed the entry porch, the buildings, the storerooms, the upstairs rooms, the inside rooms, and the room for the ark’s lid, where sins were forgiven.{c}

Every design the Spirit had given David{d} was in those plans. They covered the courtyards of Yahweh’s house and the rooms that surrounded them, the treasure rooms of God’s house, and the rooms for the holy gifts.
David gave him directions for the groups of priests and Levites, for all the work of serving in Yahweh’s house, and for all the things used in worship there.
He listed the weight of gold needed for each gold object and how much silver for each silver object, whatever its use.
The gold lampstands and their lamps each had a set weight of gold. The silver lampstands and their lamps each had a set weight of silver, based on how each one would be used.
He told him the weight of gold for each table that would hold the holy bread, and the silver for the silver tables.
He listed the pure gold for the meat forks, the bowls for sprinkling and the pitchers. He gave the weight of gold for each gold dish and the weight of silver for each silver dish.
He gave the weight of purified gold for the incense altar. He also gave him the design for the golden chariot of the winged creatures whose wings spread out over the ark of Yahweh’s covenant.{e}
David said, “All these plans were written down for me by Yahweh’s hand. He helped me understand every detail of the design.”{f}

Then David told his son Solomon, “Be strong and brave, and get to work. Don’t be scared, and don’t lose heart. Yahweh God, my God, is with you. He won’t fail you or walk away from you until all the work on Yahweh’s house is done.

The groups of priests and Levites are ready for every kind of service at God’s house. Skilled workers who are eager to help will be at your side for every job. The leaders and all the people will do whatever you tell them.”

notes.text: The ark is called God’s footstool in Psalms 99:5 and 132:7.
Compare 17:14 and 29:23, where the kingdom is called Yahweh’s kingdom.
The Hebrew says “the house of the covering.” This was the gold lid on top of the ark, often called the “mercy seat” or “atonement cover” (Exodus 25:17-22).
Or “everything he had in mind.” The Hebrew can mean “by the Spirit” or “in his spirit.”
The winged creatures are cherubim. They are pictured as God’s chariot throne (compare Ezekiel 1 and 10).
Or “Yahweh’s hand was on me, and he made it all clear to me in writing.” The Hebrew is hard to understand.

verses.text: Then King David spoke to everyone gathered there. “God has chosen my son Solomon, and him alone,” he said. “But Solomon is young and has not had much experience. The job ahead is enormous. This great building is not for any human being. It is for Yahweh God.{a}

I have worked as hard as I could to supply what is needed for my God’s house. I have gathered gold for the things made of gold, silver for the silver things, bronze for the bronze, iron for the iron, and wood for the wooden things. I have also gathered onyx stones and gems to set in metal, shiny black stones and stones of many colors, every kind of valuable jewel, and piles of white marble.{b}
Besides all this, I love my God’s house so much that I am giving my own private treasure of gold and silver for it. This is in addition to everything I have already gathered for the holy temple.
I am giving about 112 tons of the finest gold, from Ophir, and about 262 tons of pure silver. It will overlay the inside walls of the temple buildings.{c}
It will be used for the gold and silver objects and for everything the skilled workers make. Now, which of you is willing to give yourself to Yahweh today by offering a gift?”{d}
Then the leaders of families and of Israel’s tribes stepped forward and gave freely. So did the commanders of thousands and of hundreds and the officials who managed the king’s work.
For the work on God’s house they gave about 188 tons of gold, plus about 185 pounds of gold coins.{e} Silver came to about 375 tons, bronze to 675 tons, and iron to some 3,750 tons.{f}
Everyone who had jewels gave them to the treasury of Yahweh’s house. Jehiel from Gershon’s family took charge of them.{g}
The people were full of joy because their leaders had given so freely. They had given to Yahweh gladly and with all their hearts. King David was also overjoyed.
Then, in front of everyone, David praised Yahweh. “Blessed be you, Yahweh,” he prayed, “God of Israel, our forefather, for all time and beyond!{h}

Yahweh, greatness belongs to you, and power and glory, victory and splendor. The skies above and the earth below, with all they hold, are yours. Yahweh, the kingdom is yours. You are lifted high as ruler over everything.{i}
